```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# Bounds in the text are rounded outward, so that they stay true.
up <- function(x, digits = 2) num(ceiling(x * 10^digits - 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
```

Two trials can have the same informativeness and still differ in what
partial pooling does to their sites. In one, every site is about equally
reliable. In another, a few precise sites stand next to many noisy ones.
In this vignette we take the between-site standard deviation
$\sigma_\tau$ as known and study the reliabilities themselves. We look at
how the informativeness averages them, what the dispersion and the
concentration count add, and how all four summaries change with
$\sigma_\tau$, using the geometry of @lee2026 without deriving it.

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

Site $j$'s reliability is $S_j = \sigma_\tau^2 / (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)$,
where $v_j$ is the sampling variance of the site's estimate, and a trial's
reliability profile is the set of its $J$ reliabilities. See
`vignette("poolinfo")` for why $S_j$ is both a reliability and the
shrinkage weight of the normal model.

## Five profiles with the same informativeness

Our examples come from the data set `example_profiles`, with the sampling
variances of five artificial trials of 40 sites each and the reliabilities
that they give at $\sigma_\tau = 0.2$. All five have the informativeness
$I = 0.3$. They differ in their logit variance $V$, the variance of the
logits $\mathrm{logit}\, S_j$ with divisor $J$. Because
$\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j$, $V$ is also the
variance of the log sampling variances, and it does not change with
$\sigma_\tau$. The five profiles are

- `homogeneous`, in which every site has the same sampling variance, so
  that $V = 0$;
- `even`, with log variances spread evenly;
- `bimodal`, with two groups of 20 sites, one precise and one noisy;
- `concentrated_precise`, with 8 precise sites and 32 noisy ones;
- `concentrated_noisy`, with 32 precise sites and 8 noisy ones.

Apart from `homogeneous`, all have $V = 1.5$. R's `var()` divides by
$J - 1$ instead and gives
`r num(with(example_profiles, var(log(se2[profile == "even"]))))` for
them.

We make a profile of each trial with `reliability_profile()`, from its
sampling variances and $\sigma_\tau$, and collect the five profiles with
`compare_profiles()`.

```{r profiles}
by_shape <- split(example_profiles, example_profiles$profile)
profiles <- lapply(by_shape, function(d) {
  reliability_profile(se2 = d$se2, sigma_tau = 0.2)
})
cmp <- compare_profiles(.list = profiles)
cmp
```

```{r profile-facts, include = FALSE}
tab <- as.data.frame(cmp)
rownames(tab) <- tab$analysis
uneq <- tab[-1, ]
val <- function(p, q) tab[p, q]
stopifnot(
  all(abs(tab$I - 0.3) < 1e-12),
  all(abs(uneq$V - 1.5) < 1e-12), tab["homogeneous", "V"] == 0,
  abs(tab["homogeneous", "J_eff"] - 40) < 1e-9,
  abs(tab["homogeneous", "H"]) < 1e-12,
  val("concentrated_noisy", "H") == min(uneq$H),
  val("concentrated_precise", "H") == max(uneq$H),
  val("concentrated_noisy", "mean") == max(uneq$mean),
  val("concentrated_precise", "mean") == min(uneq$mean),
  val("concentrated_precise", "J_eff") == min(tab$J_eff),
  val("concentrated_noisy", "J_eff") == max(uneq$J_eff),
  abs(val("even", "H") - val("bimodal", "H")) < 0.005,
  abs(val("even", "mean") - val("bimodal", "mean")) < 0.01,
  abs(val("even", "J_eff") - val("bimodal", "J_eff")) < 0.5
)
```

In every row $I = 0.300$, while the mean reliability runs from
`r num(val("homogeneous", "mean"), 3)` in the homogeneous profile to
`r num(max(tab$mean), 3)`. Although the four unequal profiles have the
same logit variance, their dispersions range from
`r num(val("concentrated_noisy", "H"), 3)` to
`r num(val("concentrated_precise", "H"), 3)` and their concentration
counts from `r num(val("concentrated_precise", "J_eff"), 1)` to
`r num(val("concentrated_noisy", "J_eff"), 1)`, against 0 and 40 for the
homogeneous profile. Of the four, the profile with 8 noisy sites has the
smallest dispersion and yet the largest mean reliability,
`r num(val("concentrated_noisy", "mean"), 3)`. Its mirror image, with 8
precise sites, combines the largest dispersion with the smallest mean
reliability among them, `r num(val("concentrated_precise", "mean"), 3)`.
So a larger dispersion need not come with a larger gap between the mean
reliability and $I$ [@lee2026]. In every column the even and bimodal
profiles are close to each other.

Sorting the reliabilities of the two concentrated profiles shows where
these differences come from. We put the two in one comparison, to use
again below, and plot their sorted reliabilities in one panel.

```{r two-shapes, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "The sorted site reliabilities of the profiles with 8 precise and with 8 noisy sites, in one panel. In the first, 32 sites lie below the informativeness and 8 far above it; in the second, 8 lie far below it and 32 above it. A horizontal line marks the informativeness of both, 0.3."}
two <- compare_profiles(
  `8 precise` = profiles$concentrated_precise,
  `8 noisy` = profiles$concentrated_noisy
)
plot(two, type = "profile")
```

```{r two-facts, include = FALSE}
Sp <- profiles$concentrated_precise$S
Sn <- profiles$concentrated_noisy$S
stopifnot(length(unique(signif(Sp, 8))) == 2L,
          length(unique(signif(Sn, 8))) == 2L,
          sum(Sp < 0.3) == 32L, sum(Sn > 0.3) == 32L)
```

With 8 precise sites, the other 32 sit together at `r num(min(Sp))`,
below $I$, and the precise ones at `r num(max(Sp))`. In the profile with 8
noisy sites it is the other way around, with 32 sites at `r num(max(Sn))`,
above $I$, and 8 at `r num(min(Sn))`. In each profile the few sites lie
far from $I$ on the logit scale and the many lie close to it on the other
side, so that the logits average to $\mathrm{logit}\, I$.

## Three averages of the reliabilities

On the logit scale, the informativeness is the plain average of the
reliabilities,

$$
\mathrm{logit}\, I = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{logit}\, S_j,
\qquad
I = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM}(v)},
$$

where $\mathrm{GM}(v)$ is the geometric mean of the sampling variances.
Because the logits are $\log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j$, averaging them
averages the log variances, which gives the second form.

@lee2026 [Theorem 1] shows that $I$ is also the value $p$ that minimizes
the average Kullback-Leibler divergence

$$
\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}.
$$

We call the minimizer of such an average a centroid of the
reliabilities. This
divergence is one of the Bregman divergences, and two others give the
other familiar means. With $p$ in the first argument, as above, squared
error gives the arithmetic mean $\bar S$, and the Bregman divergence of
the Burg potential $-\log p$ gives the harmonic mean, our harmonic
centroid. With $p$ in the second argument, all three divergences give
$\bar S$. `reliability_centroids()` returns the three first-argument
centroids, and we apply it to each profile.

```{r centroids}
centroids <- sapply(by_shape, function(d) reliability_centroids(d$reliability))
round(t(centroids), 3)
```

```{r centroid-facts, include = FALSE}
ce <- t(centroids)
ce_uneq <- ce[-1, ]
stopifnot(all(ce_uneq[, "harmonic"] < ce_uneq[, "I"]),
          all(ce_uneq[, "mean"] > ce_uneq[, "I"]),
          all(abs(ce["homogeneous", ] - 0.3) < 1e-12))
```

In the four unequal profiles the harmonic centroid, from
`r num(min(ce_uneq[, "harmonic"]), 3)` to
`r num(max(ce_uneq[, "harmonic"]), 3)`, lies below $I$. It is never
larger than the other two, in any profile, and the three are equal only
when all the reliabilities are, as in the homogeneous profile. Between $I$
and $\bar S$, however, there is no general order. Here $\bar S > I$ in all
four unequal profiles, the sign of $1 - 2I$. A profile close enough to
constant must have that sign when $I \ne 1/2$, but a profile far from
constant can have the other. @lee2026 gives one with 25 sites and
$I = 0.3$, where one site is far more precise than the other 24, which
are all alike. We build it from its centered logits
$\Delta_j = \mathrm{logit}\, S_j - \mathrm{logit}\, I$, with mean 0 and
variance $V = 2$.

```{r counterexample}
delta <- c(sqrt(48), rep(-sqrt(1 / 12), 24))
S <- plogis(qlogis(0.3) + delta)
reliability_centroids(S)
```

```{r counterexample-facts, include = FALSE}
cents <- reliability_centroids(S)
stopifnot(abs(mean(delta)) < 1e-12, abs(mean(delta^2) - 2) < 1e-12,
          abs(cents[["I"]] - 0.3) < 1e-12,
          cents[["mean"]] < cents[["I"]])
```

Its mean reliability, `r num(cents[["mean"]], 3)`, is below $I$ although
$I < 1/2$. In the next section we give a condition that guarantees the
sign of $1 - 2I$.

## The dispersion and the gap between the averages

The dispersion $H$ is the smallest value of the average divergence above,
reached at $p = I$,

$$
H = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\},
$$

the average divergence of $I$ from the site reliabilities. It is 0 only for
a constant profile.

The sign of the gap $\bar S - I$ matters for the site effects. If
$\sigma_\tau$ and the mean effect were known, the normal model would give
the site effects an average posterior variance of
$\sigma_\tau^2(1 - \bar S)$ [@lee2026, Proposition 2]. Equally reliable
sites with the same $I$ would give $\sigma_\tau^2(1 - I)$, so a positive
gap means a smaller average posterior variance than theirs, and a negative
gap a larger one.

Both $H$ and the gap have leading terms proportional to the logit
variance $V$. With $\rho_3 = J^{-1}\sum_j |\Delta_j|^3$, the third
absolute moment of the centered logits, Proposition 2 of @lee2026 gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
H &= \tfrac12 I(1-I)V + R_H, &
|R_H| &\le \tfrac{\sqrt3}{108}\,\rho_3,\\
\bar S - I &= \tfrac12 I(1-I)(1-2I)V + R_S, &
|R_S| &\le \tfrac{1}{48}\,\rho_3.
\end{aligned}
$$

When the gap's leading term is larger than its bound in absolute value,
the gap has the sign of $1 - 2I$. `local_terms()` gives, for $H$ and for
the gap, the exact value, the leading term and the bound, and a logical
column, `holds`, that is `TRUE` when the leading term is the larger. We look first
at the bimodal profile.

```{r local-bimodal}
local_terms(by_shape$bimodal$reliability)
```

```{r local-bimodal-facts, include = FALSE}
lb <- local_terms(by_shape$bimodal$reliability)
mb <- logit_moments(by_shape$bimodal$reliability)
stopifnot(all(lb$holds), lb$exact[2] > 0,
          abs(lb$exact[1] - lb$leading[1]) < lb$bound[1])
```

For this profile the gap's leading term, `r num(lb$leading[2], 3)`, is
larger than its bound, `r num(lb$bound[2], 3)`, so the gap is positive,
as $1 - 2I$ is, and its exact value is `r num(lb$exact[2], 3)`. Since $H$
is never negative, its bound measures instead how close the leading term
is. Here $H = `r num(lb$exact[1], 3)`$, within `r up(lb$bound[1], 3)` of
`r num(lb$leading[1], 3)`.

With 8 precise sites the leading terms are the same, because $I$ and $V$
are, but a few of the centered logits are large, and $\rho_3$ rises from
`r num(mb[["rho3"]])` to
`r num(logit_moments(by_shape$concentrated_precise$reliability)[["rho3"]])`.

```{r local-precise}
local_terms(by_shape$concentrated_precise$reliability)
```

```{r local-precise-facts, include = FALSE}
S_p <- by_shape$concentrated_precise$reliability
lp <- local_terms(S_p)
ratio <- lp$exact[2] / lp$leading[2]
rem <- lp$exact[2] - lp$leading[2]
# The remainder of the gap, site by site, and its part from the 8 precise
# sites.
m0 <- qlogis(kl_centroid(S_p))
d0 <- qlogis(S_p) - m0
I0 <- plogis(m0)
r0 <- plogis(m0 + d0) - I0 - I0 * (1 - I0) * d0 -
  I0 * (1 - I0) * (1 - 2 * I0) * d0^2 / 2
top8 <- order(S_p, decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
lx <- local_terms(S)
stopifnot(
  lp$holds[1], !lp$holds[2], lp$exact[2] > 0,
  all(abs(lp$leading - lb$leading) < 1e-12),
  ratio > 0.25, ratio < 0.3,
  abs(mean(r0) - rem) < 1e-12, abs(sum(r0[-top8]) / 40) < 0.05 * abs(rem),
  !lx$holds[2], lx$bound[2] > 3 * lx$leading[2], lx$exact[2] < 0
)
```

Now the gap's bound, `r num(lp$bound[2], 3)`, is larger than its leading
term, `r num(lp$leading[2], 3)`, and `holds` is `FALSE`, so the leading
term alone does not fix the sign. The gap is still positive, but at
`r num(lp$exact[2], 3)` it is only `r pct(ratio)`% of the leading term.
Its remainder, `r num(rem, 3)`, cancels most of the leading term and comes
from the 8 precise sites, whose logits lie far above the rest. In the
profile of 25 sites the bound is `r num(lx$bound[2], 3)`, more than three
times the leading term, and there the remainder reverses the sign.

Site $j$'s term of $H$,
$\mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}$, is the
divergence of $I$ from that site's reliability. `kl_contributions()`
returns the terms, and `plot_contributions()` plots them in increasing
order, here for the profile with 8 precise sites.

```{r contributions, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Each site's term of the dispersion H for the profile with 8 precise sites, in increasing order, with H as a dashed line. The 32 other sites have small terms and the 8 precise sites much larger ones."}
plot_contributions(profiles$concentrated_precise)
```

```{r contribution-facts, include = FALSE}
kc <- kl_contributions(S_p)
share_top <- sum(kc[top8]) / sum(kc)
stopifnot(length(unique(signif(kc, 8))) == 2L, all(kc[top8] == max(kc)),
          share_top > 0.8, share_top < 0.85)
```

Each of the 8 precise sites has a term of `r num(max(kc), 3)`, against
`r num(min(kc), 3)` for each of the other 32, so these 8 sites account
for `r pct(share_top)`% of $H$.

## Changing the between-site standard deviation

The sampling variances fix the centered logits,
$\Delta_j = \log \mathrm{GM}(v) - \log v_j$, and $\sigma_\tau$ moves all
the logits together. As $\sigma_\tau$ grows from 0, $I$ grows from 0 to
1, and along this path the derivative of $H$ with respect to the logit of
$I$ is the gap $\bar S - I$ [@lee2026, Proposition 2]. So $H$ rises from 0
while the mean reliability is above $I$, reaches its largest value where
the gap is 0, and falls back to 0. To see how far the summaries move, we
compute the profile with 8 precise sites at four values of $\sigma_\tau$
with `update()`.

```{r along}
precise <- profiles$concentrated_precise
sigmas <- c(0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3)
along <- sapply(sigmas, function(s) {
  update(precise, sigma_tau = s)$stats[c("I", "mean", "gap", "H", "J_eff")]
})
round(cbind(sigma_tau = sigmas, t(along)), 3)
```

```{r along-facts, include = FALSE}
al <- as.data.frame(t(along))
stopifnot(diff(range(al$H)) < 0.025, al$gap[1] > 0, al$gap[4] < 0,
          all(diff(al$J_eff) > 0), al$I[3] < 0.5, al$mean[3] < al$I[3])
```

Over this range $H$ stays between `r num(min(al$H), 3)` and
`r num(max(al$H), 3)`, while the gap changes sign, from
`r num(al$gap[1], 3)` to `r num(al$gap[4], 3)`, and the concentration
count rises from `r num(al$J_eff[1], 1)` to `r num(al$J_eff[4], 1)`. At
$\sigma_\tau = 0.25$ the mean reliability, `r num(al$mean[3], 3)`, is
below $I = `r num(al$I[3], 3)`$ although $I < 1/2$, as in the profile of
25 sites.

`profile_path()` follows the whole path with the centered logits held
fixed, and for a profile it also gives $\sigma_\tau$ at each point. On a
fine grid we find where $H$ is largest.

```{r peak}
path <- profile_path(precise, n = 2001)
path[which.max(path$H), c("sigma_tau", "I", "H", "gap")]
```

```{r peak-facts, include = FALSE}
top <- path[which.max(path$H), ]
gm_precise <- exp(mean(log(precise$se2)))
gap_at_I <- function(I) {
  update(precise, sigma_tau = sqrt(gm_precise * I / (1 - I)))$stats[["gap"]]
}
peak_I <- uniroot(gap_at_I, c(0.3, 0.5), tol = 1e-13)$root
between <- seq(peak_I + 1e-6, 0.5 - 1e-6, length.out = 101)
stopifnot(all(vapply(between, gap_at_I, 0) < 0), abs(top$I - peak_I) < 5e-4)
stopifnot(top$I > 0.3, top$I < 0.5, abs(top$gap) < 1e-3,
          sum(diff(sign(path$gap)) != 0) == 1, path$gap[nrow(path)] < 0)
```

At the peak, $H = `r num(top$H, 3)`$,
$\sigma_\tau \approx `r num(top$sigma_tau)`$ and
$I \approx `r num(top$I)`$, and the gap is 0 up to the spacing of the
grid. So the peak is not at $I = 1/2$, where the gap's leading term
changes sign. `plot_gap_path()` plots $H$ and the gap along the path, with
their leading terms.

```{r path, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Two panels along the informativeness from 0 to 1 for the profile with 8 precise sites. The dispersion H peaks before I = 1/2, at the point where the gap between the mean reliability and I crosses 0. The dashed leading terms peak and cross 0 at I = 1/2."}
plot_gap_path(precise)
```

In the left panel $H$ rises steeply from 0, peaks at the cross and returns
to 0 at $I = 1$, while its leading term (dashed) peaks at $I = 1/2$. In the
right panel the gap crosses 0 at the same $I$, about `r num(top$I)`, and
stays negative up to $I = 1$. For every $I$ strictly between this peak
and 1/2, this profile has $\bar S < I$, against the sign of its leading term.
The point on each curve is the profile at $\sigma_\tau = 0.2$, before the
peak. A much larger $\sigma_\tau$ would bring all the reliabilities close
to 1, where $H$ and the gap return to 0. Along every path with unequal
sampling variances the gap changes sign once, because $H$ is strictly
concave in $I$ when the centered logits are fixed. With equal sampling
variances both $H$ and the gap are 0 throughout. `vignette("implementation")` gives the
argument.

## The concentration count

With the proportions $q_j = S_j / \sum_k S_k$ of the total reliability,
the concentration count is the inverse of the sum of their squares,

$$
J_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_j S_j)^2}{\sum_j S_j^2}
= \frac{1}{\sum_j q_j^2}.
$$

Its largest value, $J$, belongs to profiles of equally reliable sites,
and it approaches 1, without reaching it, as one site's proportion
approaches 1. It depends only on the proportions. A trial whose
40 sites all have reliability 0.05 and one whose 40 sites all have 0.95
both have $J_{\mathrm{eff}} = `r num(concentration_count(rep(0.05, 40)), 0)`$.

```{r count-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(abs(concentration_count(rep(0.05, 40)) - 40) < 1e-9,
          abs(concentration_count(rep(0.95, 40)) - 40) < 1e-9)
```

We plot the cumulative proportions of the two concentrated profiles, the
most reliable sites first, with `plot()` and `type = "concentration"`, a
call to `plot_concentration()`. Because the 8 precise sites are tied, we
leave out the labels that would name the most reliable sites.

```{r concentration, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "The cumulative proportion of the total reliability against the fraction of sites, most reliable first, for the profiles with 8 precise and with 8 noisy sites, with the diagonal of equal proportions. The first curve climbs steeply over the first fifth of the sites; the second climbs a little faster than the diagonal and flattens after four fifths of the sites."}
plot(two, type = "concentration", label_top = 0)
```

```{r concentration-facts, include = FALSE}
q_top8 <- sum(sort(Sp, decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]) / sum(Sp)
q_top32 <- sum(sort(Sn, decreasing = TRUE)[1:32]) / sum(Sn)
stopifnot(q_top8 > 0.5, q_top8 < 0.55, q_top32 > 0.975, q_top32 < 0.985,
          max(Sn) / sum(Sn) > 1 / 40, max(Sn) / sum(Sn) < 1.3 / 40)
```

With 8 precise sites the curve climbs steeply over the first fifth of the
sites, which carry `r pct(q_top8)`% of the total reliability, and then
rises slowly. With 8 noisy sites it climbs evenly, a little faster than
the diagonal, until the 32 precise sites have contributed
`r pct(q_top32)`% of the total, and the 8 noisy ones add the rest. The
concentration counts printed in the panel,
`r num(val("concentrated_precise", "J_eff"), 1)` and
`r num(val("concentrated_noisy", "J_eff"), 1)`, summarize the two curves.
To see which sites carry the reliability in your own analysis, you can
give a posterior fit to `plot_concentration()` and `plot_contributions()`
as well.

## The geometry in two plots

Each site's term of $H$ is a Bregman divergence. With
$\phi(p) = p \log p + (1 - p)\log(1 - p)$, the term
$\mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}$ is the height of
$\phi$ at $I$ above the tangent to $\phi$ at $S_j$. `plot_geometry()` shows
the curve, the tangents at a few sites and these heights. We use the even
profile, whose 40 reliabilities all differ, and four of its sites spread
over the range.

```{r geometry, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Panel (a): the curve p log p + (1 - p) log(1 - p) with the tangents at four sites of the even profile and, at p = I, the vertical gap between the curve and each tangent. Panel (b): the four gaps as bars."}
even <- profiles$even
plot_geometry(even, sites = c(1, 14, 27, 40))
```

```{r geometry-facts, include = FALSE}
drawn <- c(1, 14, 27, 40)
ke <- kl_contributions(even$S)[drawn]
de <- qlogis(even$S) - qlogis(kl_centroid(even$S))
stopifnot(identical(order(even$S[drawn], decreasing = TRUE), 1:4),
          identical(order(ke, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2], c(1L, 4L)),
          abs(de[1] + de[40]) < 1e-12, even$S[1] > 0.3, even$S[40] < 0.3,
          all(abs(de[c(14, 27)]) < abs(de[1])))
```

In panel (a) the longest gap belongs to the most reliable of the four
sites, at `r num(even$S[1])`, and the next longest to the least reliable,
at `r num(even$S[40])`. These two sites are equally far from $I$ on the
logit scale, but the divergence is not symmetric, and the site above $I$
has the larger term. Between them, the sites at `r num(even$S[14])` and
`r num(even$S[27])` are closer to $I$ and have short gaps. Panel (b) gives
the four terms as bars, `r num(ke[1], 3)`, `r num(ke[2], 3)`,
`r num(ke[3], 3)` and `r num(ke[4], 3)`. Their mean is not $H$, the
average over all 40 sites.

Theorem 2 of @lee2026 splits the average divergence of a constant
reliability $p$ from the profile into two parts,

$$
\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^J \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\}
= \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(p) \,\|\, \mathrm{Ber}(I)\} + H,
$$

so the average is smallest at $p = I$, where it equals $H$.
`plot_decomposition()` plots the left side against $p$ and shows the split
at one value of $p$, here 0.75.

```{r decomposition, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "The average divergence of a constant reliability p from the even profile against p, with its minimum H at p = I, the mean reliability marked just to its right, and the split at p = 0.75 into the divergence of p from I plus H."}
plot_decomposition(even, at = 0.75)
```

```{r decomposition-facts, include = FALSE}
kl <- function(p, q) p * log(p / q) + (1 - p) * log((1 - p) / (1 - q))
I_e <- kl_centroid(even$S)
H_e <- kl_dispersion(even$S)
at_avg <- mean(kl(0.75, even$S))
at_kl <- kl(0.75, I_e)
sbar_avg <- mean(kl(mean(even$S), even$S))
stopifnot(abs(at_avg - at_kl - H_e) < 1e-12, mean(even$S) > I_e,
          sbar_avg > H_e, sbar_avg - H_e < 0.01)
```

The curve's minimum, at $I = 0.3$, is $H = `r num(H_e, 3)`$, the height
of the dashed line. At $p = 0.75$ the average divergence is
`r num(at_avg, 3)`, of which `r num(at_kl, 3)` is the divergence of 0.75
from $I$ and the rest is $H$. The mean reliability, `r num(mean(even$S), 3)`,
sits just to the right of the minimum and a little above it on the curve.
It minimizes the average with $p$ in the second argument, a different
function of $p$.

## Making profiles of your own

You can build profiles like these with `shape_profile()`, for a
simulation or to see what the diagnostics of a planned trial might look
like. It returns sampling variances with a given number of sites,
informativeness, logit variance and shape at a given $\sigma_\tau$. Here we
ask for 20 sites in two groups, with $I = 1/2$ and $V = 1$.

```{r shape}
v <- shape_profile(J = 20, I = 0.5, V = 1, shape = "bimodal",
                   sigma_tau = 0.25)
half <- reliability_profile(se2 = v, sigma_tau = 0.25)
half
```

```{r shape-facts, include = FALSE}
hs <- half$stats
lh <- local_terms(half$S)
stopifnot(abs(hs[["I"]] - 0.5) < 1e-12, abs(hs[["mean"]] - 0.5) < 1e-12,
          length(unique(signif(half$S, 8))) == 2L,
          abs(sum(qlogis(half$S))) < 1e-9,
          hs[["H"]] > 0, abs(hs[["H"]] - lh$leading[1]) < 0.01)
```

Its reliabilities take two values, `r num(min(half$S))` and
`r num(max(half$S))`, whose logits lie symmetrically around
$\mathrm{logit}\, I = 0$. At $I = 1/2$ the gap's leading term is 0, and
for this symmetric profile the mean reliability equals $I$. Yet
$H = `r num(hs[["H"]], 3)`$, close to its leading term
$\tfrac12 I(1 - I)V = `r num(lh$leading[1], 3)`$, so two equal centroids
do not make the reliabilities equal.

`vignette("planning")` starts instead from the site sizes, and
`vignette("posterior-summaries")` returns to an estimated $\sigma_\tau$.
